newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG ministers resign, PM Chan pressured to quit.
newsitem.headline: PNG ministers resign, PM Chan pressured to quit.

text.p: Ministers in the cabinet of Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan resigned en masse on Monday, piling yet more pressure on Chan to quit over his hiring of foreign mercenaries.
Five ministers either resigned or promised to resign and they said at least four others were expected to join them ahead of a parliamentary resolution against Chan on Tuesday.
Chan is facing a motion to force him to resign over a $36 million contract with the British firm Sandline International for mercenaries to crush a rebellion on Bougainville island.

The army has also set Chan and two close allies a deadline to quit before parliament resumes on Tuesday afternoon and earlier on Monday the South Pacific nation's governor-general, Sir Wiwa Korowi, also urged him to step aside.
Three of the ministers who are quitting are senior members of Chan's People's Progress Party, including Agriculture Minister David Mai and Lands Minister Sir Albert Kipalan.
Kipalan backed the army in its demand that Chan, his deputy Chris Haiveta and defence minister Mathias Ijape should resign.
"If the three of them don't go, then we will go," Kipalan told Reuters on Monday evening. "More are expected to follow."

A tearful Mai said he was resigning because he did not want to be part of a decision that was made against the best interests of the nation and people. He urged other political leaders to do the same.

Mai said the decision to hire the mercenaries was never discussed at either cabinet or parliamentary level and as such it had been illegal. The secret contract was signed by Haiveta in January and provoked international condemnation when it became public last month.
"I have five children and I want to do the best for them and for my country." Mai said. "It is with great regret that I tender my resignation.

The crisis, the worst in Papua New Guinea's 22 years of independence, began a week ago when army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok turned against Chan and demanded that he terminate the mercenary contract and quit.
Chan sacked the general and tried to ride out the storm but Singirok, popular among his troops, remained in effective control of the army and let violent street protests pile the pressure on Chan.

Members of the opposition, which includes former prime ministers Sir Michael Somare and Paias Wingti, said they would support a motion in parliament on Tuesday that would force Chan to resign and install a caretaker government before elections already set for June.
The British commander of the mercenaries, retired colonel Tim Spicer, appeared in court on Monday and pleaded not guilty to two firearms charges.
Spicer, who served with the British army in conflicts around the world and was a high-ranking U.N. peacekeeper in Bosnia, will be unable to leave the country before his trial on April 8.
"I don't think we would have done anything different," Spicer said after his court appearance, adding: "It's unfortunate the way things have turned out."
Ahead of Tuesday's vote, parliament became a focus for protest. About 150 demonstrators staged a sit-in outside the building and protest leaders promised thousands on Tuesday.
The week-long crisis has preoccupied Papua New Guinea's Pacific neighbours.
Australia, its former colonial power, has had troops on standby to help around 10,000 Australians living in the country if the situation deteriorates.
Malaysian High Commissioner Mohamad Sani said his mission had plans in place in case an evacuation was needed and New Zealand said it was working on contingency plans to evacuate its nationals.
